name.text: Graphing a linear inequality passing through the origin

questiontext.text:
Solve and graph the following linear inequality in two unknowns:

\( \displaystyle y < {@m@}x \)

a) Find the \(y\)-intercept of the boundary equation \( y = {@m@}x \), and determine the corresponding \(y\)-value when \(x = {@x_val@}\).

(Enter the numerical values below.)

\(y\)-intercept (when \(x = 0\)): \( y = \) [[input:ans1]]

\(y\)-value when \(x = {@x_val@}\): \( y = \) [[input:ans2]]

\(y\)-intercept check: [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]
Second point check: [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

b) Graph the inequality on the Cartesian plane below:

  • Drag the two blue points to set the boundary line. (Notice the line is dashed because the inequality is strict: \(<\)).
  • Drag the green Region Marker into the area that satisfies the inequality \( y < {@m@}x \).

generalfeedback.text:
Worked Solution:

Part a: The Algebraic Boundary

To plot the boundary line \( y = {@m@}x \), we need to find two coordinate points.

First, we find the \(y\)-intercept by substituting \( x = 0 \):

\( \displaystyle \begin{aligned} y &= {@m@}(0) \\ y &= 0 \end{aligned} \)

Because the line passes exactly through the origin \((0,0)\), the \(x\)-intercept is also \(0\). We must evaluate a different \(x\)-value to find a second point. Substituting \( x = {@x_val@} \):

\( \displaystyle \begin{aligned} y &= {@m@}({@x_val@}) \\ y &= {@ta2@} \end{aligned} \)

The boundary line passes through \((0, 0)\) and \(({@x_val@}, {@ta2@})\).

Part b: Graphical Representation

We plot our two points on the Cartesian plane and draw a dashed line through them because the inequality is strictly less than (\(<\)).

Next, we determine which region to shade using a test point. Because the boundary line passes through the origin \((0,0)\), we cannot use it as a test point. Instead, we select a point clearly off the line, such as \((1, 0)\). Substituting \(x = 1\) and \(y = 0\) into our inequality:

\( \displaystyle \begin{aligned} y < {@m@}x \\ 0 < {@m@}(1) \\ 0 < {@m@} \end{aligned} \)

This statement {@test_statement@}. Therefore, we place our region marker on the {@shade_direction@} side of the dashed line as the point \((1,0)\) to indicate the shaded area.
